context_blurb:
Much of what you touch is a mix. Seawater, soil, air and brass are each several substances mingled together. Chemists sort all matter into two big groups, pure substances and mixtures, and knowing which is which tells them how a material will behave and how its parts can be pulled apart.

A pure substance is just one substance, with the same make-up and the same properties wherever it comes from. It comes in two kinds. An element, such as gold or oxygen, is made of only one kind of atom, the tiny building block of matter, and it cannot be broken down into anything simpler. A compound is two or more elements joined chemically in a fixed ratio, making a new substance. Only a chemical reaction, a change that makes new substances, can split a compound apart.

The ancient Greeks counted water as an element, beside earth, air and fire. In 1800, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle passed an electric current from a battery through water, and it split into two gases, hydrogen and oxygen. Since electricity breaks water into simpler substances, water is a compound of the two. The bubbles in boiling water are different: they are only water vapour, water as a gas.

Charcoal is mostly carbon, and as it burns, its carbon joins chemically with oxygen from the air. The two always combine in the same fixed ratio, so burning charcoal gives off carbon dioxide, a compound of carbon and oxygen: one new gas, not the two old elements simply mingled. Carbon dioxide is also one of the gases you breathe out.

In a mixture, the substances are not joined. They mingle in any amounts, and physical means such as filtering or settling can sort them out again. A homogeneous mixture is the same all the way through, like air or salt water. Brass, the golden metal of many wind instruments, is a homogeneous mixture: copper and zinc melted together, with the zinc spread evenly all through the copper. A heterogeneous mixture is uneven, and you can often see its different parts, like the coloured grains in a speckled rock.

Soil is a heterogeneous mixture you can test yourself. Shake a few handfuls with water in a clear jar until it is all mud-brown, then leave it alone for two or three days. Its grains of sand, silt and clay do not dissolve, so they settle out by size: sand, the biggest, within a minute, silt within a couple of hours, and the tiny clay grains last, over a day or more. So the jar ends up in layers, with sand at the bottom and clay on top, under clear water.

A thermometer can tell a pure substance from a mixture. A pure substance boils at one fixed temperature: at sea level, pure water always boils at 100 degrees Celsius. A mixture's boiling point depends on what is in it. Dissolved salt raises the boiling point, so seawater, with salt dissolved in it, boils a little above 100, at about 100.6 degrees.

Panning for gold separates a mixture by density, which means how heavy a material is for its size. Gold is many times denser than sand: about seven times denser than quartz, the main mineral in sand, and about nineteen times denser than water. So as the panner swirls water through the gravel, the lighter grains wash out over the edge while the gold sinks and stays. A tiny gold flake weighs far less than a pebble; it stays because gold is so heavy for its size.

In everyday talk, pure can mean that nothing was added, but to a chemist a pure substance is one single substance. Water from a mountain spring has seeped through rock underground and dissolved calcium, magnesium and other minerals from it. With rock minerals dissolved in it, spring water is a mixture, however clean and natural it is.
